h.strategy: Most obvious hypotheses follow a local story: an option matters more when its substitute is missing. These are usually rated likely and often fail. Instead, base hypotheses on robust statistical regularities. (1) Headroom: helpful edits help less in parents that are already strong, for example parents that already contain the strongest option elsewhere. (2) Harmful edits hurt more in strong parents and look harmless in weak parents, because of floor effects. (3) Saturation: adding a second copy of a strong option gives smaller gains than adding the first. (4) Removing an option costs less when the parent has several similar options. Choose conditions that many parents satisfy, so the effect is detectable. Cover several edited fields and both directions. In each 'why', state the obvious prediction and the reason the opposite should hold.

hyps.why: Obvious: removing edge 5 hurts most when node 3 has few inputs; but a parent already weak is at the floor, so the extra removal costs little.
Obvious: removal hurts connectivity; but in an already sparse parent the floor effect makes the removal nearly harmless.
Obvious: dropping the direct edge hurts; but a parallel strong conv3x3 path into node 3 makes the removal cheaper due to redundancy.
Removing an edge into the output costs less when a strong parallel edge into node 3 already exists.
Saturation: a second skip into node 3 adds less than the first.
Headroom: a helpful skip adds less when node 2 is already fed by a strong conv.
Headroom: parents already containing conv3x3 elsewhere gain less from an additional conv3x3.
Saturation: the second copy of the strongest op adds less than the first.
Saturation: a second conv1x1 in the cell yields a smaller increment than the first.
Saturation: with strong conv3x3 already feeding node 3, an extra conv1x1 on the direct edge adds little.
